rationale: This policy and institutional case study examines the implementation of Ecuador's 2008 constitutional human right to water and sanitation. Two governance mechanisms are co-central (`assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple` = `multiple`): (1) `institutional_structure_coordination` (primary), analyzing how SENAGUA fails to operate as a single coordinating water authority amidst overlapping mandates, policies, and uncoordinated public investments across MIDUVI, MAE, MSP, INAR, and 219 municipalities; and (2) `regulatory_model_ownership`, examining constitutional mandates for exclusive public and community management versus ongoing private franchises/concessions (e.g., INTERAGUA in Guayaquil, Amagua in Samborondon, private solid waste services, multilateral privatization programs) and the integration of 9,952 community water systems (JAAPRE), alongside secondary discussion of `participation_assistance` in water governance. On the outcome side (`assigned_outcome_label_with_multiple` = `multiple`), the paper primarily tracks `primary_connection` (national, urban/rural, regional, and socioeconomic trends in residential piped water and public sewer connections from census and survey reports) while also substantially evaluating `effective_access` (service continuity/permanence at 33%, wastewater treatment rates, water quality, and project sustainability). The study design is `qualitative`, synthesizing constitutional/legislative analysis, ministerial management and project evaluation reports (e.g., PRAS), and secondary official descriptive statistics without original statistical modeling.
